newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Long bond tug-of-war.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Long bond tug-of-war.

text.p: U.S. debt markets will likely stay rangebound Wednesday as late-month portfolio squaring and fresh economic data are expected to keep the 30-year bond yield trapped between 6.35 and 6.40 percent, analysts said.
"It's a tug-of-war between the month-end buying, which is going to have to come in, versus some fundamental news," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
Pulling at one end of the rope are money managers, who usually wait till the end of the month to buy the long end of the yield curve to adjust their portfolios.

The opposing side, seen as more bearish, believes the long bond is overpriced and might use Wednesday's new home sales report as an excuse to sell, if the data suggest, as expected, that the economy remains healthy.
June new home sales data will be released at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. The report is expected to have dipped slightly in June, but economists remain optimistic about the housing sector.

Experts surveyed by Reuters said new home sales are expected to decline to an annualized rate of 818,000 from May's 825,000. Annualized sales above 800,000, economists said, hints at a healthy housing industry.
Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc, said new homes sales can be very unpredictable.

"It is certainly possible that we can get one of those 850,000 readings that would shock the market a little bit," he said. "I doubt it could have a long-term affect, but it would roll things in the other direction," he added.

Market players will also receive the Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement of three-year notes, 10-year notes and 30-year bonds, at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT. Last quarter's refunding totaled $39 billion.
Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Inc, said he is calling for a $38.5 billion refunding effort.
He said he expected a slight cutback in the size of the refunding because of the strong Treasury balances and rising tax receipts. "The Treasury just doesn't need to raise that much money," he said.
Among Federal Reserve official speeches, central bank Governor Edward Kelley is scheduled to testify Wednesday at a Senate Banking committee's hearing at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
In late trade Tuesday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 8/32 at 103-05/32, to yield 6.38 percent, the lowest yield since December 3, 1996.
The 10-year bond was up 6/32 to yield 6.10 percent, while the two-year note gained 3/32 to yield 5.79 percent.
The federal funds rate was seen opening at 5.63 percent on Wednesday, above the central bank's 5.50 percent target.
